text: Edward Maurice Charles Marsan OBE (born 9 June 1968) is an English actor who won the London Film Critics Circle Award and the National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance in the film Happy-Go-Lucky (2008). He was born in the Stepney district of London to a working-class family; his father was a lorry driver and his mother was a school dinner lady and teaching assistant. He was raised in Bethnal Green and attended Raine's Foundation School. He left school at 16 and initially worked as a printer before starting his career in theatre. Marsan trained at the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, graduating in 1991, and later studied under Sam Kogan at the Kogan Academy of Dramatic Arts, now known as The School of the Science of Acting, of which he is now a patron. His first year at drama school was funded by Mr Benny, a bookmaker who ran a menswear shop where Marsan worked; he received scholarships for the remainder of the course. It took many attempts for Marsan to secure a place at drama school. His first television appearance was in 1992 as a "yob" in the London Weekend Television series The Piglet Files. One of his more significant early television roles was in the mid-1990s BBC sitcom Game On, where he played an escaped convict who was an old flame of Mandy's. He went on to appear in Casualty, The Bill, Grass, Kavanagh QC, Grange Hill, Silent Witness, Ultimate Force, Southcliffe, and more. He also voiced the Manticore in the Merlin episode "Love in the Time of Dragons". In 2011, he starred alongside Olivia Colman and Peter Mullan in the British drama film Tyrannosaur. In 2013, he began portraying Terry Donovan, the brother to the lead character in seven series and 82 episodes of Showtime's drama series Ray Donovan, and also played Ludwig Guttmann in the television film The Best of Men. In May 2015, he appeared as the practical magician Gilbert Norrell in the BBC period drama Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell. His film roles include the main villain in the 2008 superhero film Hancock alongside Will Smith, as Inspector Lestrade in Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes, and other films such as Sixty Six, Gangs of New York, 21 Grams, The Illusionist, V for Vendetta, Gangster No. 1, Miami Vice, Mission: Impossible III, I Want Candy, Vera Drake, Happy-Go-Lucky, Filth, Tyrannosaur, and Heartless. In 2021, he played anti-Fascist activist Soly Malinovsky in the television adaptation of the novel Ridley Road. In 2022, he portrayed the real-life John Darwin in ITV's drama series The Thief, His Wife and the Canoe. In 2024, he appeared as Mitch Winehouse, father of Amy Winehouse, in the biopic Back to Black. Marsan married make-up artist Janine Schneider in 2002; they have four children. He is a humanist and was appointed a patron of Humanists UK in 2015. In 2015, he criticized the lack of representation of working-class people in the arts on BBC Radio 5 Live, stating that too much drama is written from "the white, privileged, middle class perspective". In 2024, he was interviewed on HARDtalk in an episode entitled "Do the arts neglect working-class people?". Marsan was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2025 New Year Honours for service to drama.
